Reported Speech and Questions

You use reported speech (indirect speech) when you are saying (reporting) what other people said.
This style of writing is common in storytelling. It allows the writer to share dialogue with the reader without always using quotation marks.

When you tell people what someone has said you generally make the verb tense 'more in the past' since we are reporting the information at a later time. You need to change the verb to the next past form.
For example:

{"rows":6,"columns":2,"cells":["{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Direct speech\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Reported speech\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"“I love him.” \"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"She said she loved him.\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"“I'm coming to the party.” \"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"He said he was coming.\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"“I already drank.” \"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"He said he had already drunk.\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"“I can speak English.” \"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"He told me he could speak English.\"}"],"styles":" intro_table_border instruction_table_background"}
You have to change the pronoun if you are reporting what someone else said. Compare these two sentences. In each case the person actually said "I don't want to go."

• I said, “I don't want to go.” > I said I didn't want to go.
  • Beth said, “I don't want to go.” > Beth said she didn't want to go.
When you want to report questions asked, the subject normally comes before the verb.

Direct: The frog asks Hansel “Where are you going?”.
Indirect: The frog asks Hansel where he was going.
When the question is a yes/no question, you use if or whether to report it.
The father asks his sons if/whether they have found wives.

The Passive: The Present Continuous and Present Perfect Tenses

You use the Present Continuous to talk about an action that is happening at the time of speaking. The action or event is in progress.
People are pushing them to marry.

You use the Present Perfect to talk about a finished action or event with present consequences. There is a connection between what happened in the past and the present.
This tale has been told by people in my family for ages.
You often choose the passive form when you want to talk about an action but are not so interested in saying who or what does/did it. Passives without agents (the doers) are common in storytelling.
Look at the chart below for the structure of the passive voice.

images.text:
This tale has been told by people in my family for ages.

There is a father with three sons. They are being pushed to marry. They have been sent out to look for wives. They've been told not to come back without one.

One son, Hansel, is not the brightest bulb in the box. While passing a pond, he's being watched by a frog. The frog asks Hansel where he was going. Like ... who hasn't been asked a question by a frog, right?
Hansel explains that he was looking for a wife. The frog jumps onto a leaf and asks Hansel if it could marry him. Simple Hansel says that, yes, he could marry the frog and treks home.

The father asks his sons whether they have found wives. He jumps for joy as he is being told that each of them has. He says that he would give the family abode to the son who brought home the most beautiful wife.

Each son feels that the beautiful wife has already been found. (I told you that Hansel was none too bright. He considers his frog a beauty!)

So, the frog in the pond has been asked to go back to Hansel's house as Hansel's future wife. (Perhaps Hansel has been told the story of the frog prince!) The frog is very happy.

Hansel has been given three keys and told to take them to a castle and take what he wants from the rooms they open.
